Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

rmoriebricklayer 1.0.0

Fixes after the CRAN resubmission

  • An error raised while co2fp() measures a computation’s footprint is now named after the function that asked for the footprint (for example cpschk: the provenance names no source to fetch), not after co2fp().
  • The vignettes run their code again wherever they are built (r-universe, pkgdown, R CMD build), so the articles show their plots; only R CMD check re-building a vignette skips the computing.
  • The package installs faster: the C++ sources build as one compilation unit, so the headers they share are compiled once. To make that possible, code that several files had copied is now shared: the Keccak sponge state (declared in five places), the arbitrary-precision helpers of the RSA and decimal parsers (where the RSA parser’s comparison now also holds for numbers with leading zero limbs), the hex encoders and a bit rotation; the C++ sources include R’s headers with R_NO_REMAP, and the size checks use C++ static_assert.
  • The 0.5.x names are no longer R functions (except the eleven rmoriedata 0.3.x calls and the four S3 generics): the rmbl command line translates them instead, with the new verbs run and migrate, and describe and examples now answer for an old name. Every exported function has an example.
  • Code nothing calls is gone: an unused jsonlite-style layer (minify, prettify, read and write files, stream, rbind pages, flatten; about 410 lines that no function of the package reached), the helpers of the removed 0.5.x wrappers, and three unused credentials and certificate helpers. The tests that guarded live behaviour through them now call the functions the package uses (fromjs() for the JSON parser’s errors, the URL validator for host classification, the credentials reader). Two statements after a return() or break were rewritten so that no code is unreachable.
  • The 33 print methods that print an object’s format() lines share one function instead of 33 copies of the same body; yoy_summary() has one method where two were identical.
  • Checks that {goodpractice} runs: %||% is defined once (it is base R from 4.4.0, and defined only for older R) instead of in four files; print() of a 0.5.x-form result returns it invisibly; two on.exit() calls add to the exit handlers instead of replacing them; the four test seams (the AES and HQC backend switches, the running mean, the services memo) live with the tests instead of in the package; the DESCRIPTION no longer uses two dependency names as ordinary words; and a test helper named dbl(), which {lintr} mistook for rlang::dbl() and crashed on (so that none of its checks ran), is now hexdbl().
  • The README and the DESCRIPTION now say first, in plain words, what the package is for: analyzing a table someone else publishes, pinning the data a result came from, and signing the record. The README says why it exists and shows how it is used, with code that runs.
  • README: three examples used 0.5.x argument names (anltab(period =, rounding =), recrd(observed =, expected =, synthetic =), wrsmrytxt(what_was_done =)) and one read a renamed field ($any_drift, now $anydrft, which printed NULL); every R block of the README now runs as written.
  • Help pages: quoted words and phrases use \dQuote{}, so the PDF manual prints an opening and a closing quotation mark instead of two closing ones, and quoted values are in code font (\code{"mean"}). A percent sign written in a help page’s text no longer cuts off the rest of its line (in 11 pages, for example the 50% rule in ?cnsprof, which read “50" and stopped).
  • Spelling: US spelling throughout (“optimized”, “renormalized”, “victimized”), code names in code font, and the technical terms in inst/WORDLIST; spelling::spell_check_package() finds nothing.
  • R CMD check no longer reruns the vignettes’ analyses: when it re-builds a vignette, only the setup chunk runs. R CMD build, r-universe and pkgdown still build every vignette in full, so the package carries each one’s HTML, figures and R code.
  • The 33 guides are now five vignettes, one per theme: vignette("capsules-and-provenance"), vignette("integrity-and-cryptography"), vignette("describing-data-and-tables"), vignette("statistical-methods") and vignette("applied-analyses"). Each former guide is a section of one of them, with its text, code and figures unchanged.
  • Every example runs in GitHub CI, on r-universe, on the package website and in an interactive session (for example with example()), and the full test suite runs in GitHub CI and on r-universe. On CRAN, to keep the check within its time limit, the help pages show every example but R CMD check runs only those of csha256() and keyeddgst(), and the tests run their fast core.
  • Every vignette now draws its results: the 21 that had no figure gain one or more, drawn with the package’s own plot() methods and plot helpers from the objects each vignette builds.

A dashboard, distributions and proof ledgers

  • rmblapp() opens a dashboard over the package’s analyses on your own machine (rmbl app [PATH] [--port N] [--no-browser] from a terminal; it needs shiny, which is suggested, not imported). Load a CSV file, a capsule’s pinned data or a data.rmorie.com table, then describe, compare years, compute rates, test trends, estimate from a survey, fit distributions, check a capsule, evaluate a policy on a panel, read the First Nations, Metis and Inuit tables, work through courts and corrections counts, model a plume and its burden, fit a Hawkes process, or check a proof ledger. Each analysis shows the R call it ran and runs exactly that call; a refusal is shown in the package’s words with explerr()’s note. The Report tab gathers results into one HTML page (plots as inline SVG), Markdown or a GitHub comment. vignette("dashboard").
  • The dashboard is built with bslib (suggested, and installed with shiny): menus in the navbar, a form in each tab’s sidebar, value boxes with the estimate, its interval, n and a verdict, a plot card that opens full screen and downloads as PNG, SVG or CSV, a method card (the method in its help page’s words, its assumptions, what the numbers mean, how to read the effect sizes), a diagnostics card, the table and the R call. Every tab opens with its first analysis run on a demo dataset. Resampling analyses run in the background so the page stays live, refusals also show as a notice, a column of the profile opens its distribution, the year-over-year plot shows a period’s rows on hover, the Drift tab gives each snapshot’s share of a brushed range, and “Share this view” bookmarks the page in its URL. Dark mode follows the switch in the navbar.
  • rmbldemo() returns seeded, made-up datasets for the dashboard and examples: a court caseload panel with a staggered reform, monthly offence counts with a step change, a stratified survey with replicate weights, a published health table with suppressed cells, custody stock and flow, a monitor series around a plume source, a Hawkes event stream, two drift snapshots, case processing times and a proof ledger.
  • dstfit() fits normal, log-normal, exponential, gamma, Weibull, Student t, Pareto, beta, Poisson, negative binomial and zero-inflated Poisson and negative binomial distributions by maximum likelihood in base R, ranks them by AIC with BIC, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Anderson-Darling statistics, gives percentile bootstrap intervals and a Hill tail index, and plots the density, QQ, PP and log-log tail. mksyncol() takes type = "fitted" to draw from a fit.
  • New plots in the house style, each returning what it drew: plotrdg() (ridgelines), plotecdf(), plotvln() (violins), plothex() (hexagonal bins), plotgain() (concentration curves), plotcal() (calendar heatmap), plothrz() (horizon chart), plotsm() (small multiples) and plotbump() (ranks over time). plothwk() draws a fitted Hawkes process’s intensity, time-rescaling check and most probable branching; chwksim() simulates from it.
  • ldgrread() and ldgrchk() read and check a proof ledger (schemapath("ledger")): each theorem proved with no sorry, each covered function exported by the installed package, each numeric check within its tolerance. A check is evaluated in a sandbox that allows only the named package’s functions and base arithmetic, so system() or a file read is refused before it runs. A capsule whose provenance says kind: "ledger" gets these rows, and its commit and build pins, from rmbl verify.

Standards and the fixes they surfaced

  • The package documents the rOpenSci statistical software standards (General, EDA, Time Series) with srr tags: 149 standards tagged as met, 29 not applicable, none left to do.
  • A period with no percentage change in plot(yoy(...)) carries its whole reason again (“first period: nothing to compare with”, “no percentage: previous period is zero”), sized to the panel; the period-axis rewrite had cut every reason at the colon.
  • The plots over time put the period on its own scale (a number or a Date; text at labelled positions) with the unit as the axis title, and take xlab, which passed through ... was an error. plot() of a yoy() or ratechg() result draws the period across and the change up, with vertical interval bars; groups sit side by side. gaps = "break" (the default) breaks a line at a missing value, such as a “no data” year yoy() inserted, and gaps = "join" draws over it.
  • A refusal that several functions share now starts with the name of the function that refused ("anltab: data must be a data frame"), and so do the shared argument checks.
  • stepchg() puts before, after and difference back into the units of y when the series is above 1e150 (they stayed rescaled), rescales a series below 1e-150 as well (the squares underflowed and every split tied), and refuses an x that is not numbers or dates, has a missing period or is not strictly increasing. trndtst() refuses duplicated periods.
  • yoy() compares yearly, quarterly and monthly Date periods (all on one day of the month, or all month ends) on a grid of calendar months; on a grid of days none of them had a comparison.
  • svydes(type = "jkn") on a domain keeps a replicate that deletes a PSU of a stratum of 101 or more PSUs: its factor, within 1% of the weight, is the 1 / rscale its rscales says, and it was refused as a copy.
  • The plots over time put text periods in time order (fiscal years, years, year-months, quarters), not in the order they first appear. plot(yoy(...)) says “no data in the previous period” for a period after a gap, which it called the first period, and refuses a result with no values.
  • rtcalc() and ratechg() name pop in their refusal, and exprspplr() names the call estr(data, y, expo, confs). blcli() refuses NA or a function as args, dlogin() a function as email, and instcli() a dir it cannot create or write, each with its name in front.
  • The examples that sign keep the one-time index record in a temporary file, and the slower examples of blcli() and explerr() run only in an interactive session.
  • chwkfit() warns when the branching ratio sits on its 0.99 bound.
  • yoy() compares ordered-factor periods by level order and completes missing levels; its refusal names every accepted input. fylbl()’s help says a fractional year is an error.
  • Every internal function has a roxygen2 block with @noRd (srr G1.4a).
  • Plot labels shrink to no less than 0.6 of the session cex (?blpal).
  • cpsatst(), cpsbndl() and their checks take a shared secret (HMAC, the attestation recording only its key id), so bundles signed by morie verify with cpsbndlvrf(key = ).
  • README: who the package is for, which algorithms re-implement existing packages and are checked against them, the life cycle, and how to run the extended tests.

Capsule template and the attestation check

  • vrfcps() reports a provenance record that does not parse as a failed provenance_readable row with the parser’s message, instead of stopping; the other rows are then run as for a missing record. morie.capsule.verify() answers the same way.

  • usecpstmpl()’s analysis.R pins the source digest into data_provenance.json on its first run (source$sha256 and a resource block), so vrfcps() verifies the capsule from then on. Before, the provenance said the digest would be filled in and nothing ever did.

  • cpschkatst()’s key_as_expected row says whether the key matched; its detail read the same either way.

  • The Docker image installs the package and puts rmbl on the PATH.

  • capenv()$packages is a named list, so a manifest written with wrmnfjs() keeps the package names; as a named character vector they were written as a bare array of versions.

Drift you can look at

  • plot() of a cpsdrft() result takes what: "psi" (the default) draws the PSI per column, worst first, coloured by verdict with the warn and fail bands as dashed lines; "columns" draws the reference and current distributions of up to six columns (cols) with each PSI bin’s term; "benford" the first digits of numeric columns against Benford’s law with its 95% band; "ecdf" the two ECDFs, "quantiles" the quantile shift and "fingerprint" the PSI of every column on spokes, the bands as rings.
  • cpsdrft() keeps a binned summary of each column (summ: missing shares, summary statistics or the largest categories, the PSI bins, a histogram, first-digit counts; never the rows) and its PSI bands, which the plots and reports colour by.
  • drfthtml() writes the drift report as one HTML file that fetches nothing: the verdict and provenance; the chosen column’s two distributions drawn in on a canvas; a column table to search, filter and sort; per column its statistics and the density overlay or category flow, ECDF overlay, quantile shift, PSI by bin and Benford charts, each with a line on how to read it; the drift fingerprint and a tile per column; the manifest diff as a tree; PSI over earlier runs as a heatmap; the capsule chain (provenance, bytes, manifest, attestation); sliders for the bands and alpha that score every chart again; and Markdown, JSON, SVG and GitHub-comment exports. Dates show in ISO 8601. rmbl drift PATH --html FILE writes it.
  • drftapp() is the same report as a Shiny app (shiny is suggested), with what would clear a column, a rerun on chosen columns and a download of the page; drftapp() alone opens on two uploaded CSV files, and rmbl drift PATH --app opens it on a capsule whose source moved. cpschk() keeps each capsule’s cpsdrft() result in its drifts attribute.

Capsule checks from the command line

The checks the rmbl GitHub Action ran in its own script are now in the package, so the action can call them.

  • rmbl verify PATH checks every capsule under PATH: each capsule file against its JSON Schema, then vrfcps() and cpsbndlvrf(), one row per check, with the action’s Markdown report. --json prints the rows as JSON instead, and --fail-on error|drift|warn sets which failed row makes the exit status 1. The secret of an HMAC bundle is read from RMBL_KEY, which is removed from the environment at once; --public-key pins the signing key.
  • rmbl drift PATH verifies, then fetches each source again: new bytes are a warning, and columns that drift (cpsdrft()) are drift. rmbl refresh PATH pins the new bytes, and rmbl report PATH [--format md|json] prints the verify report and never fails.
  • The schemas ship in inst/schemas/ (the same files as the action’s spec/); schemapath() gives their path.
  • mnfdiff() lists the resources two manifests (provenance records, bundles or data frames) added, removed or changed, with their digests and sizes.
  • cpsrfrsh() fetches a capsule’s source again and, when the bytes changed, writes them and pins them in the provenance as usecpstmpl()’s analysis.R does; it returns the mnfdiff().
  • dload() takes token, a MORIE key for that call that is used in place of the stored one and never printed. (key is already the table’s name.)
  • explerr() takes a data frame of check rows, as rmbl verify --json writes them, and explains each failed row.
  • cpschk() runs these checks from R, and with them everything the action’s script computed on its own: PSI bands (psiwarn, psifail; --psi-warn, --psi-fail) with the action’s verdicts, the per-column drift table with the Benford first-digit p-values of the pinned and the new data, each manifest compared with its base copy (base, --base: a manifest file, a folder, or a function that resolves a git ref; results through mnfrcmp(), resources through mnfdiff()), a cache of fetched sources read when a fetch fails (cache, --cache; none outside an interactive session unless a folder is given), file:// sources (allowfile, --allow-file), Wayback snapshot rows (snapshot, --snapshot) and captures on refresh (wayback), a glob over the capsule files (glob, --manifests), explerr() notes on every failed row, and the footprint of the checks (co2fp()) at the foot of the report (fp, --no-footprint). format() renders the Markdown report or the JSON.
  • ghann(), ghcmt() and ghout() turn a cpschk() result into GitHub workflow annotations (the file, and the line of a schema problem), the body of a sticky pull-request comment and the action’s step outputs. They return text; nothing in the package calls GitHub.
  • In rmbl drift, new bytes whose columns all stay within the PSI bands are a note rather than a warning; new bytes that cannot be compared column by column are still a warning.
  • cpsrfrsh() records resource$retrieved_utc, takes allowfile for a file:// source, and refuses new data that fail the schema the provenance pins.
  • rmbl sign PATH pins each plain provenance on its first run and signs each capsule into capsule_bundle.json (cpsseal()), then verifies, so a program in any language only writes the data and a provenance naming it. The key is RMBL_KEY or the contents of --key-file, never printed: the shared secret for --scheme hmac (the default), or for a standardised scheme the JSON of a fipskg() key or its secret hex with --public-key. An existing bundle is refused without --overwrite.
  • rmbl sign --scheme xmss-sha256 --key-file key.json signs with an XMSS key and treats the key file as its state, as RFC 10033 asks: before anything is signed the file is rewritten atomically (a temporary file beside it, flushed and renamed, under a lock) with next_index advanced and a used field holding the highest index used, a generation counter and a digest of the host that wrote it. A key file that cannot be rewritten is refused; --state-file keeps the state elsewhere, and a key in RMBL_KEY needs it. --sectors K --sector-index I (or --sector NAME) signs only in one of K disjoint index ranges, --reserve N reserves N indices in one write, --warn-left N warns when the range is nearly used up, and a key file older than a signature it is seen to have made (in a bundle under the path, or in the --seen-log each run appends to) is refused as a stale copy. The command line never writes to the configuration directory; RMBL_XMSS_INDEX_FILE is used only when it is set.
  • rmbl verify and cpsbndlvrf() name each XMSS signature’s index and key fingerprint, and an index one key signed twice under the path or in --seen-log (cpsbndlvrf(seen = ), cpschk(seenlog = )) is a failed xmss_index row. xmssidxseen() lists the XMSS signatures in a folder of bundles and seen-logs and marks a reused index. cpsseal() signs several capsules with one XMSS key, at consecutive indices.
  • The capsule checks compare manifests with a base folder by paths relative to the folder searched on every system, and the smoke test restores what its drift case changed, so a Windows path no longer reaches rmbl refresh as a file:// URL.
  • plot() of a rtcalc() result with period draws the period on its own scale, as the other plots over time do, and takes xlab; it drew index positions with no axis title.

Short names

Every exported function, argument, output column, help topic and option now has a short name without underscores (survey_design() is svydes(), conf_level is conflvl, trend_sensitivity() is tse()). Each help page gives the full form of every short name. The 0.5.13 names that 1.0.0 renamed are known to the command line, which translates them: rmbl describe admissions says what the name became and shows its page, rmbl run admissions --adp 120 --alos 30 calls the function by its old name with its old argument names and values, and rmbl migrate script.R rewrites a 0.5.x script to the 1.0.0 names (--write writes it). Renamed allowed values ("mean_bootstrap" is "meanboot", "higher_is_better" is "higher", "all_cause_mortality" is "allcause") and old argument names passed through ... are translated too. In R, the eleven functions rmoriedata 0.3.x calls keep their old names (?rmbl-compat), and so do the four S3 generics below; ?rmbl-aliases lists every renamed value, column and field. The nine options read their 0.5.x names too (rmoriebricklayer.xmss_index_file for rmoriebricklayer.xmssidxfile), so a record or cache an old .Rprofile points to is still used. rate(), rate_change(), share() and yoy_summary() stay S3 generics, so methods written for them still dispatch. yoy() kept its name and takes its 0.5.x argument names (period, min_base, conf_level, direction) beside the new ones. Results of the four generics come back under their 0.5.x column and field names (co2e_g, pct_valid, nested tables and attributes too, and the header row of a delimited writer), and print(), plot(), format() and summary() work on them. A 1.0.0 call returns the 1.0.0 names. The one call that cannot tell is yoy(), which kept its name: with a 0.5.x argument name it returns the 0.5.x names, without one the 1.0.0 names (pctchg for pct_change); ?rmbl-aliases lists every renamed column and field. rmbl functions and the help-aware language-model tools list the new names. Wire formats (capsule, manifest and service JSON fields, CSV columns from published tables) keep their names, so files written by earlier versions still read.

First Nations, Metis and Inuit health, mental health and wellness

Methods for the published tables, distinctions-based (First Nations, Metis and Inuit are each reported on their own), with suppressed cells never imputed. Data governance follows OCAP® and the CARE Principles: only openly licensed aggregate tables are used, and First Nations-held survey data are not mirrored. A new vignette, “First Nations, Metis and Inuit health: published tables, distinctions and governance”, covers them all.

Reading the tables

  • sctidy() reads a Statistics Canada table as published. VALUE becomes a number, and the quality flag is kept beside it. F, x, .. and ... cells are NA.
  • scests() puts each estimate beside its confidence limits and count.
  • indtabs() lists the tables the data service mirrors: the 233 Indigenous-titled Statistics Canada tables, and the 2021 Census Indigenous Population Profile.
  • indiex() bundles four published excerpts (tables 13-10-0924, 41-10-0067, 41-10-0082 and 41-10-0021), so the examples run on real values.

Comparisons

  • indgap() gives the difference and ratio against a reference group.
  • dstntst() tests whether the groups differ before they are pooled (Cochran’s Q and I²).
  • ordcmp() compares rated scales, such as perceived mental health or life satisfaction, as whole distributions: the probability of a higher rating, with an interval from the published limits.
  • agestd() and rategap() cover counts. stdprev() covers survey percentages.
  • genexpo() and exptrnd() cover the intergenerational effects of the residential schools.
  • trcind() maps each indicator of Call to Action 19 (health gaps) and Call 55 (children in care, education, income) to the tables that measure it. trchlthgap() measures every gap against non-Indigenous people on one scale, “times worse”, with intervals. Life expectancy and infant mortality (tables 17-10-0160 and 17-10-0161) are bundled for it.
  • trccmpl() and trcprog() track the 94 Calls to Action, as the Yellowhead Institute counts them (Jewell and Mosby).

Estimators built from Indigenous scholarship on mental wellness

These translations are ours. They are inspired by the scholars’ work, which is largely qualitative, and are not taken from it as stated methods. Each help page says so, and says what the estimator cannot show.

  • Prof. Suzanne L. Stewart:
    • welprof() reports wellness beside distress, strengths first (Stewart 2008, 2020).
    • holbal() measures how evenly wellness is held across a person’s domains: the ratio of the geometric to the arithmetic mean, with community-set weights and Monte Carlo intervals (Stewart 2008; Gabriel, Mirza and Stewart 2022).
    • dualcont() treats wellness and distress as two axes (with Keyes 2002, 2005).
    • healchg() reads change between survey periods as healing in process (Stewart 2008).
  • Prof. Angela Mashford-Pringle:
    • connassoc() measures connection to land, community and education across places: Spearman’s rho with an exact permutation p-value, and an interval that carries the published sampling error (Mashford-Pringle and Stewart 2019, Akiikaa; Mashford-Pringle 2016).
  • Other frameworks:
    • mhcont() covers the First Nations Mental Wellness Continuum’s four directions (hope, belonging, meaning, purpose) from published proxies. A direction with no proxy is said to have none.
    • commidx() combines protective and risk factors with weights the community sets, after the National Inuit Suicide Prevention Strategy. The function never chooses the weights.
    • cwbscr() computes Indigenous Services Canada’s Community Well-Being index.
    • frmaud() gives the share of a report that is deficit-framed (Walter’s 5D data).

The 2021 Census Indigenous Population Profile

  • cnsprof() reads the profile. It keeps the characteristic hierarchy, the full-count or 25% sample of each topic, the residence (on or off reserve), and the suppression symbols. Repeated labels are told apart by their member number.
  • profshr() gives shares (for example foster children among children, or speakers of an Indigenous language) with intervals that carry the long-form sample and random rounding.
  • cnsstd() gives an Indigenous standard population for age standardisation.
  • cnscwb() computes a Community Well-Being score from the public profile, and says where it departs from the Department’s method.
  • Two real excerpts (indiex("census_population") and "census_households") make every example and test run on published values.

Every result draws itself with plot().

Any agency’s table, and the review of every estimator

  • limfrom() builds limits from a standard error, a coefficient of variation or a margin of error, and qltyrcd() maps another agency’s flags onto suppressed and use-with-caution. An unknown flag warns and counts as ok.
  • Published limits that miss their own estimate warn, and that estimate is set aside, in every estimator.
  • indgap(), ordcmp() and dstntst() take pooled_groups; the output column pan_indigenous is now pooled_group. Duplicate groups are refused, and a total as the reference warns.
  • scests() turns a coefficient of variation into log-normal limits, which stay above 0.
  • holbal() refuses proportions and gives a bias-corrected interval that holds the estimate.
  • stdprev() takes scale (100 by default, Inf for rates).
  • genexpo() takes partial: a known attendance beside an unknown one is NA by default, or 1 as a lower bound.
  • connassoc() gives a Monte Carlo p-value of (b + 1) / (R + 1) beyond eight places; its band is documented as a sensitivity band.
  • healchg() takes distress; other indicators are marked "other".
  • commidx() keeps its conf_level.
  • profshr() takes rounding_base; on reserves, where the long form was a full canvass, there is no sampling term.
  • cnscwb() matches places by DGUID and takes min_population (250 by default; the Department uses 65). Its doc says that housing is pooled across Indigenous households.
  • cnsstd() takes a DGUID where place names repeat.
  • trchlthgap(): times_worse is now disadvantage_ratio. It takes reference, and warns on duplicate rows.
  • rategap() refuses a group against itself; exptrnd() refuses an outcome with no variation.
  • The README, the vignette and the pages of the estimators acknowledge Professors Suzanne Stewart and Angela Mashford-Pringle, on whose frameworks they are built.

Fetching what the Wayback Machine cannot capture

  • fetchvrf() fetches a file from its source (with the source’s own Wayback fallback) or from any mirror, and keeps only a copy whose SHA-256 is the one pinned. For servers that refuse the Internet Archive’s crawler (Statistics Canada does), a capture made elsewhere and published as a mirror serves the same verified bytes.
  • arccap() makes that capture: it fetches each URL from here, records its SHA-256 in a manifest, timestamps the manifest with an RFC 3161 authority (verified with tsvrf()), and uploads the files, the manifest and the timestamp as one public archive.org item, streamed from disk with a new libcurl PUT. Given a wbsave() result it takes the URLs whose server refused the Internet Archive.

Evaluating a policy from administrative panels

New estimators, each checked against the reference implementation (fixest, did, bacondecomp) to rounding error, in base R:

  • plndid(): difference in differences with two-way fixed effects and CR1 cluster-robust errors (one-way or two-way), weights, linear combinations with delta-method errors (the effect after a phase-in), and the effect relative to the comparison units’ pre-period mean.
  • evstudy(): leads and lags around adoption, with the joint Wald test of the leads.
  • stgatt(): group-time effects for staggered adoption (Callaway and Sant’Anna, with not-yet-treated or never-treated comparisons; or Wooldridge’s extended two-way regression), aggregated overall and by time since adoption, with a cluster bootstrap.
  • bacondcmp(): the two-way estimate split exactly into its two-group comparisons.
  • swtdid(): de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille’s estimator, with its placebo.
  • perminf() and stpdnpv(): Fisher’s test by re-assigning adoption dates across clusters (every assignment when there are few), and Westfall-Young stepdown p-values for several outcomes.
  • plnpois(): fixed-effects Poisson or negative binomial (NB2, base R) for counts, as rate ratios.
  • synctl(): one treated unit against a convex combination of donors, with the placebo-in-space test.
  • sevidx(), piperate(), cmlrisk() and bufasgn(): the measures these designs take from justice data.
  • polex() and the vignette “Evaluating a policy from administrative panels”. The designs are those of Professor Angela Zorro Medina’s empirical work.
  • stgatt() takes covariates: doubly robust, IPW or regression difference in differences per cohort and period (Sant’Anna and Zhao 2020), equal to did::att_gt().
  • perminf() and the wild bootstrap take ties ("count" or "strict").

Causal estimation on panels

  • plndml(): double machine learning with unit and period fixed effects (Clarke and Polselli 2025), cross-fitted by unit, with base-R lasso, ridge or OLS learners or any learner function, a second-order basis built before demeaning, repeated splits, and cluster-robust errors; equal to DoubleML given the same folds.
  • aipwcf(): cross-fitted augmented inverse probability weighting for a binary treatment (average effect, or effect on the treated) with survey weights and propensity clipping; the average effect equals DoubleML’s interactive regression model given the same folds. With design = svydes(...) the standard error comes from the design’s replicate weights (any replicate type) or strata and PSUs, from one fit: the learners are fitted without the weights, so each replicate estimate is the replicate-weighted mean of the same cross-fitted scores, equal to re-running on every replicate weight.
  • mtchdid() and baltab(): matching on pre-treatment trajectories (Mahalanobis, pooled within-group or full-sample covariance, exact groups, calipers), then the weighted difference in differences; matches equal MatchIt’s.
  • syndid(): synthetic difference in differences (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021) with exact weights, placebo or jackknife errors.
  • wcb(): the restricted wild cluster bootstrap with Rademacher or Webb weights, full enumeration, and an interval by test inversion that is unbounded when the design cannot reject.
  • tse(): Rambachan and Roth’s relative-magnitudes bounds with a conservative interval and the breakdown value.
  • plnpwr(): design-based power and the minimum detectable effect on real data.
  • The figures of policy papers: event studies in a Stata style or with the post-period shaded, plotevgrid() for several outcomes, the Goodman-Bacon scatter, permutation distributions, loounit() and cohtrnd().
  • sprd(): the variance, standard deviation and standard error with the correction the data call for (Bessel’s n - 1 for a sample, none for a whole population described as it is, the finite-population correction for a sample drawn without replacement, frequency or reliability weights), chosen automatically from the population size and explained.

Search and rescue

  • Search theory for planning a search, in base R: ltrlrng() (lateral range curves), swpwdth() (sweep width), srchpod() (probability of detection from coverage), pswppod() (a parallel sweep, with navigation error), srchscs() (probability of success and the update after a search that finds nothing), datumpmap() (point, line and area datums on a grid), optcrcsrch() and opteffort() (the optimal effort for a circular datum and over cells), and optsqr() (the square a point-datum search should cover, for one search or a series). The numbers agree with rmorie’s to 1e-12. Each result prints and plots, and the dashboard (rmblapp()) has a “Search and rescue” tab with them and a picker for the book’s figures. srchfig() draws each of the 36 figures of Frost’s The Theory of Search (1996) from these functions with the book’s parameters, and a new vignette, “Search and rescue”, walks the book’s chapters through them.

Fixes from the CRAN stress test of 0.5.14

  • No leak on an argument error in compiled code: an error raised inside a C++ entry point jumped over the C++ objects alive at that moment (two strings at every error of the barrier, 3,200 bytes over 50 calls under valgrind; the Merkle chunks, an NA URL with headers set, BLAKE2b with an NA element). The barrier now holds its message in a fixed buffer, and an argument error inside a body is thrown and raised by the barrier once the body’s objects are destroyed; valgrind reports nothing lost on those paths. The barrier generator (inst/scripts/gen_barrier.R) writes all of it, so regenerating the file keeps it.
  • rsvidx() answers Ctrl-C: 3e9 items ran 37.9 s through a SIGINT.
  • stepchg(): when every ordering is enumerated the observed one is among them, and is no longer counted twice (p = 73/721 for 0.1). Drawn permutations keep the +1.
  • trndtst() on a constant series gives p = 1 at every length (it was NA past n = 8).
  • cnttrnd() with zeros at one end only (c(0, 0, 5)) warns that the trend has no finite estimate and reports a rate ratio of Inf (or 0) with no interval; it was 9.7e16 silently.
  • valrules() on a table of no rows fails no row-wise rule (every rule failed).
  • onlsmry() takes each block’s sums in two passes, as var() does: values near 1e8 with a spread of 1 lost nine digits of the variance. The help page says “to rounding”, not exact.
  • Seeds: knoxtst() takes every seed up to 2^53 - 1 (2^40 was refused, -2^31 called too large), and cpsfals() records a seed past 2^31 - 1 as given (it became NA).
  • Network: the URL gate refuses 6to4 addresses that carry a private IPv4 address ([2002:7f00:1::] is 127.0.0.1), Teredo, the local-use NAT64 prefix and the discard prefix; a 307 or 308 redirect repeats a POST as a POST, to the same host only (it became a GET); wbsave() does not send the public archive a URL on your own network (https://10.0.0.7/, a .local or one-label name); the manifest is read with a 32 MiB cap (a 300 MiB gzip bomb was read whole before allocation failed).
  • JSON: a well-formed reply is parsed in compiled code (15 MiB took 85 s; 9.4 MiB takes 0.26 s). Whatever the R parser has words for (an error, a big integer, a duplicate key, nesting past 100 levels) is still parsed by it, so messages and warnings are unchanged, and a staged bundle, which has no compiled code, parses as before (its R parser is twice as fast too).
  • CSV reader parity with read.csv(skipNul = TRUE): NUL bytes are dropped before quotes are read (a quote, a NUL and a quote is a doubled quote; a line of "" with a NUL in it is blank); a quote after a closed quoted field opens a quoted run again, a comma or line end inside it being text ("x"y",z" is the one field xy,z); a byte-order mark after an empty "" in the first row is dropped. The two shapes it refuses, where read.csv() changes the data without a word (a record with more fields than the header, a quote inside an unquoted field), are now in the help page.
  • CLI: a three-letter near miss (rmbl "dat list"), a hyphenated one ("xplain-rror?") and a short line naming a file ("urls.txt?", "my urls.txt") are not questions; a run of 16 or more letters and digits mixed (an archive.org key) is a key; --model and llmask(model =) refuse a key given as a model name before any route is looked for (it was sent as the model).
  • svydes(): a post-stratified JK1 set on a post-stratum subset is accepted (the replicates that delete a PSU with no row there are the weight); the adjustment is read from the replicates that differ from the weight, and for JK1 from the factors across the set (one factor n / (n - 1) unadjusted).
  • Tests on CRAN: no test renames the installed launcher (it wrote into the library); the wall- clock bounds are fifty times wider where CRAN runs the tests (under valgrind they took 19 s against 15 and 30 s against 10); the archive.org lookup needs RMBL_LIVE_TESTS=1. The agentbndl() example points the settings folder at an empty one, so a saved key cannot make it call a provider.
  • Undefined behaviour: a NaN probability in the quantile kernel and a NaN time in the Hawkes compensator are no longer cast to an integer.
  • plots.R: the “µg” unit is a value, not a name in c(), so a non-UTF-8 locale keeps it.
  • Arguments, again: a battery of every export with 41 hostile values in every argument (not only those the examples set; 38,836 calls over 306 functions) found 1,007 base R errors in 77 functions past the fixes above (the stress test counted 1,070 in 180), among them every yoy_*() writer’s digits, stepchg(), scanadj() and the plots’ col =; each is refused in words, naming the argument (the final audit’s wider battery, 15 values in every argument of every export, found 90 more raw errors in 31 functions; those are fixed below). Shared checks do most of it: a single number in a range (.rmbl_scalar()), an environment refused where data goes, a date refused as a count (reps = Sys.Date() ran 20,000 replications), colours checked before a device sees them (one check for every plot), titles checked once. morani(n_perm = 1) no longer fails on the spread of one permutation.
  • Memory: chwkres() and the fits built a grid of one point a time unit, 32 GB for a horizon of 2^31 (the process was killed); a constant baseline needs none, a sinusoidal one keeps a point a day and refuses a horizon past 4,194,304 days. mksyncsv() refuses more than 100 million rows (it builds the table in memory; 2^31 was a process killed). svydes() computes its row keys and their digests in C and its degrees of freedom a block of rows at a time: 5e6 rows and 20 replicates peak at 2.8 GiB as a matrix and 2.4 GiB by name (3.5 and 3.1), the design in 20 s and an estimate in 5 s (52 s each in the stress test).
  • A time limit ends a loop over your function: cpsfals(), cpspwr() and the exposure-response bootstrap caught setTimeLimit()’s error as one more failed statistic and ran on.
  • The README says 123 C++ entry points behind the barrier (one new, the JSON path) and 15 in plain C (the survey column pass and the set digest are new).

After the tag: the manual, the plots, a C locale

  • The reference manual ran off the page on 123 lines: long URL templates and option names inside inline code, dense lists of code, references with long DOIs. R’s Rd.sty lets inline code neither break nor stretch, so the help text was reworded (URL templates split at a slash, references with the link on its own line, options named in prose, long lists as bullets). No line is 10pt over now; the 61 left are under 10pt, most under 2pt.
  • Plot titles of 17 methods were handed straight to the base-graphics call, so a title wider than the panel was cut (“Community Well-Being, by place and gro”). Every method now draws its title with the fitter the others use: full size, then smaller, then two lines.
  • Row labels are drawn with mtext(), sized to the row (down to 0.45), instead of axis(), which leaves out labels that would overlap: trchlthgap()’s 44 rows showed 22 labels beside the wrong points. plot.rmbl_trc_gaps() adds a key for the groups.
  • Labels cut to the same text keep the part that told them apart (“…of 8, 9 or 10” and “…between 0 and 5”) instead of a number; the wellness profile breaks long indicator names onto two lines.
  • A C locale: cnsprof() matched the profile’s column names against UTF-8 keys, so “MÉTIS” never became “Métis”, and its table of column names was built with a non-ASCII name inside c(), which a package installed in a C locale stores as M<U+00C9>TIS; .rmbl_json_parse() converted before it checked, so invalid UTF-8 was reported as an unexpected character; the CSV reader’s byte-order-mark cases are compared with read.csv() only in a UTF-8 locale, where its behaviour is defined.
  • rmoriebricklayer.allowhttp was read by the R-level URL check but the native transport still read the old rmoriebricklayer.allow_http, so bldl() refused plain http whatever the option said. Three more from the coverage pass: evstudy(leads = 1) failed with “subscript out of bounds” (no lead left to test); baltab() failed on a group of one unit (its tests are NA now, as after mtchdid() with a tight caliper); chwkfit(meth = "em") with every event at the horizon divided 0 by 0 (the branching ratio goes to its floor). mcartst() refuses an infinite value in its own words rather than as collinearity.
  • Every line of R and the reachable lines of C++ are now covered by the tests; the dead guards found by the pass are gone.
  • The statement about a third-party security audit is gone from DESCRIPTION, the README, SECURITY.md and the help pages.
  • Every example’s output was read against its comment. print.rmbl_yoy() printed “no periods” for a column subset; the cpsrpt() example read a mrkroot field that is called merkle_root; the recrd() comments say when a status is INFO instead of PASS; the onlsmry(), benfordtst(), wrmnfjs(), cpspwr() and plnpois() examples show what they claim.
  • vignette("plotting-results") gains the policy-evaluation plots, one call per result; vignette("policy-evaluation") draws the synthetic difference in differences and vignette("causal-effects") the AIPW estimate beside its overlap.

The final pre-CRAN audit (three reviewers and a re-run of every earlier finding)

  • A test failed R CMD check on a host without IPv6 sockets (a kernel booted with ipv6.disable=1): the socket guard’s probe now answers NA where the address family cannot be opened, and the test skips there instead of reading it as a refusal.
  • Large CSVs read through the streamed path (tables past 512 MiB) took a ragged row silently, the first column as row names and the data shifted one column left; read.csv()’s field count is checked record by record first, and the file is refused in the same words as the in-memory path.
  • The survey reorder check read a swap of two rows beside one edited cell as “in order” (SE 9.60 for 9.92 with no error): the design keeps one key per row, and rows that moved beside fewer rows that changed are a reorder, whatever the columns the swap left unchanged say. An edit that turned an integer column into a double one changed every row’s code as well; integer and logical columns now code as their doubles do.
  • A double column holding -0 (round(-0.3) is -0) gave its row an NA key, which wiped the other columns’ contribution and hid reorders among such rows: -0 codes as 0 and every NaN payload, NA among them, as one value. A design saved by 0.5.14 with NA in a double column is rebuilt on its data.
  • The degrees of freedom read the replicate matrix’s rank from a B x B cross-product: with more replicates than rows that asked for 74.5 GB (n = 20, B = 1e5) and took 113 s at B = 5,000. The smaller of the two Gram matrices is read, the replicates scaled first (a replicate of 1e308 overflowed eigen()).
  • Memory, again: svydes() reads each replicate column against the weight in one native pass with nothing allocated as long as the column (the R pass held 340 MB a column at 5e6 rows), and its row-key digests read a column as a set through an order-independent hash in place of a sorted copy (a radix sort asks for working memory as long as the column outside R’s heap, and that request failed at the limit). 5e6 rows and 20 replicates now fit a 3 GB address space as a matrix and by name, the matrix design in 6 s (17 before). A domain estimate centres its linearized values within strata one column at a time and reads the rows of each domain once: fifty domains at a million rows peak at 0.65 GB of heap (1.9 before).
  • The replicate contract’s edges: a Fay replicate equal to the weight (a post-stratified domain whose rows sit in one PSU per stratum) is said, not refused; one factor k/(k - 1) on every row with no row left out, carried by more or fewer replicates than its k (w * 1.005 beside 200 JKn replicates, the full data plus w * 15/14 under JK1), is said as a rescaled copy. Two or more JKn replicates equal to the weight stay as they are: a stratum left out of a subset leaves all of its replicates at the weight, and two copies of it cannot be told from that.
  • The manifest fetch capped the bytes on the wire, and a reply sent with Content-Encoding: gzip was stored as sent and decompressed whole by readLines(): 300 MiB of zeros in a 300 KB body (a 2.3 GB allocation, or an OOM kill). The manifest is read a megabyte at a time through gzcon() and refused past 32 MiB decoded.
  • The JSON fast path gave up on a big integer, a duplicate key and nesting past 100 levels and handed the whole document to the character-by-character R parser: one such value at the end of a 15 MiB reply cost minutes. Whole numbers of 16 digits or more follow the R parser’s rules in C++ (text when asked, else a double, the inexact ones warned about once), a duplicate key and deep nesting are refused there in the same words and at the same character, and any other failure in a document past 128 KiB is refused with its reason instead of re-read. The direct .Call refuses bytes that are not UTF-8 rather than handing back an invalid string, in a C locale too (R’s translation there rewrote such bytes as <ff> before the check saw them).
  • The command line: a trailing ? no longer makes a question of a near-miss command (dat list?, conifg set openai.api_key?); zero-width characters are removed before the key check, so a key broken by them is still a key; dotted or underscored runs with digits in two segments or more, sixteen letters that change case four times or more, and a key typed in groups of 8 to 16 characters are keys; a UUID, dashed groups of mixed-case characters, a 15-character mixed token or a key of a known prefix given as --model is not sent as the model name.
  • col = is checked by the field, density, Knox and leave-one-out plots (raw image() errors before; the leave-one-out plot ignored it).
  • onlsmry() refuses an infinite value in words (smrystat() failed in R’s); stepchg() reads a series near the double’s range in units of its largest value (the statistic overflowed to Inf, the p-value to NaN); fylbl(2024.5) is refused instead of labelled “2023/24”.
  • rmbl exits 130 for a Ctrl-C that lands while R is still starting (status 1 and “Execution halted” before); an interrupt a native call took and a tryCatch(error = ) swallowed as “interrupted” is raised again as the interrupt it was (rmbl data pull went on for 65 s once in ten runs).
  • The tests’ wall-clock bounds widen with the machine’s load per core and under covr; the test that connects to the loopback discard port skips on CRAN.
  • syndid() and synctl() solve their simplex-constrained least squares by an active set on the KKT system (one small solve a step) with the projected-gradient method as the fallback: the tiny ridge of the time weights ran the latter to its iteration cap, a second a placebo and 55 s of CPU in each of two vignettes; 0.04 s now, at the exact optimum (the earlier weights were the cap’s approximation, so estimates move in the third digit).
  • The hostile-argument battery, 20 values in every argument of every export, found raw base R errors in 31 functions: a NULL seed (set.seed(NULL) in seven functions), a learner function of the wrong arity, NULL column names, 1e308 in the air-dispersion arguments, block sizes, pubbnd()’s suplim and supmar, mksyncol()’s basep, tojs()’s digits, the bundle, capsule and template file arguments, yoylbl()’s labels, profshr()’s num and den, plotevgrid()’s main, plnpois()’s offset, trchlthgap()’s tables, wcb()’s trtd, chgenv()’s per, the strict and ex flags, the col of the rule*() builders and chwknll()’s par, and shrs()’s total. Each is refused in words now. The re-check of the fixes replayed the battery and found 29 more in nine functions, refused in words too: blcli()’s out, cnscwb()’s groups, dlogin()’s token, rtcalc()’s infinite counts, recrd()’s manifest, plotfnl()’s target and stkflow()’s per. A key typed in groups with punctuation on its last group ("... qrst9012uvwx?") is a key.
  • The native CSV reader drops a byte-order mark before a header name when blanks follow the mark (read.csv() keeps the mark in the name, X.s): 37 of 24,000 fuzz inputs, documented.

Fixes from the review of the native code

  • macOS: siudate() returned “” for every accented French date (“3 août 2017”, “3 DÉCEMBRE 2017”) because the native text code folded case with std::tolower(), which on macOS in a UTF-8 locale rewrites the bytes of a multibyte character as if they were Latin-1. Case folding of text that may hold UTF-8 is ASCII-only now, in the SIU parser, the SIU resolver and the transport (r-universe macOS checks of 1.0.0).
  • fetchvrf() no longer passes on R’s “cannot rename file” warning when it falls back to copying the kept file into place.
  • ECDSA verification refuses an r or s longer than the curve and a key coordinate that is not exactly one field element: r with 2^1152 added was read back as r and verified.
  • The elliptic-curve multiplication refuses a scalar longer than 144 bytes instead of reading only its low bytes.
  • A host written with a trailing dot (https://example.com./) is fetched as example.com, so the address pin and the URL libcurl is given name the same host; before, libcurl found no pin and resolved the name again itself.
  • Every connection the transport opens is checked as it opens, so a private or loopback address is refused even when it comes from somewhere other than the pin. This includes a proxy named by http_proxy or https_proxy: a proxy on the loopback interface or a private network is now refused.
  • The decimal reader is correctly rounded past 768 significant digits: dropped digits that were not all zero now count when the kept ones are exactly halfway.
  • The decimal reader takes nothing after Inf, Infinity or NaN (any case), so "Info" and "nanny" are NA, as as.numeric() reads them.
  • cgamcdf() is accurate for large shapes. At x = a it gave 0.4786 for a = 1e4 and 0.0797 for a = 1e6, where the answer is 0.5013 and 0.5001.
  • A missing, zero or negative timeout is the default for every request, never no limit at all.
  • Destinations and upload paths starting with ~ are expanded. A destination that cannot be written is reported as a local failure, without a Wayback lookup.
  • On Unix, a download that cannot be moved into place leaves the old file as it was. Only Windows removes the destination before the move.
  • The download progress callback protects both of its arguments while it builds the call.
  • An RSA signature must be exactly as long as the modulus (RFC 8017 8.2.2): leading-zero variants of a valid signature no longer verify.
  • An XMSS signature whose randomizer is not 32 bytes of hex does not verify. It used to raise an error.
  • XMSS keys name their seeds pubseed, skseed and skprf, as the help pages always said. Keys saved with the earlier pub_seed, sk_seed and sk_prf still sign and verify.
  • The Hawkes messages name the argument hor.
  • kemsz() and hqcsz() name their sizes public, secret and shared, as the keys and capsules name them. siusch() names its column count, and fipssz() names the per-signature randomness rnd.
  • The native errors name the R arguments: person and addl for the DRBG, pass for PBKDF2, rnd for SLH-DSA.
  • One-shot SHA-3 and SHAKE wipe their Keccak state. The permutation can be run backwards, so the state gave back secret inputs such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA seeds.
  • The SHA-256 and SHA-512 message schedules and contexts are wiped after use, so an HMAC key padded with ipad no longer stays on the stack.
  • XMSS key generation and signing wipe their seeds on every exit, including a refused argument or an interrupt, along with the heap buffers and chain steps derived from them.
  • The heap copies of BLAKE2b and HMAC keys, the derived PBKDF2 key and the operating system’s random buffer are wiped before they are freed. HMAC no longer frees an unwiped copy of the padded key when its buffer grows.
  • Unmasked ML-DSA signing wipes the sampler seed, the packed mask and the values of rejected attempts.
  • siuso() removes the glossary sentence in one linear pass. 8000 repeats took 28 s before.
  • siutxt() no longer rescans to the end of the page for every unclosed script or style tag.
  • The SIU parsers and the distinct-count sketch read latin1 input as the text it is: a latin1 “5 décembre 2023” is a date, and one value in two encodings is counted once.
  • siudate() refuses an impossible ISO date such as 2023-02-30 or 2023-13-45, as it already refused February 30.
  • A director whose name contains the letters “the”, such as Heather Smith, is no longer dropped.
  • A numeric entity naming a UTF-16 surrogate decodes to nothing instead of invalid UTF-8.
  • HTML entities are decoded once each, in one pass, so &amp;lt; stays the literal &lt;.
  • Lower-casing SIU text no longer passes negative values to tolower().
  • The kernels published to LinkingTo packages have the guards of their .Call versions. Theil-Sen takes at most 20,000 points and polls for a Ctrl-C, and an exception in any of them is an R error instead of ending the session.
  • Moran’s I checks its neighbour indices and nperm before it allocates, and polls for a Ctrl-C between permutations.
  • The Hawkes entry points refuse an eps or a sum-of-exponentials window that is not one. eps of NaN silently dropped the excitation term, and 0 ran out of memory.
  • The C API’s Hawkes likelihood keeps its own kernel codes and Lomax shape, now documented in the header and checked against chwknll().
  • Midranks of a vector with NaN are defined: the comparator orders NaN last.
  • The SHA-256 chunk state no longer carries four uninitialised padding bytes.
  • The Wayback snapshot URL is returned whole and with its JSON escapes undone. A long URL was cut at 2047 bytes.
  • A download whose file cannot be reopened after a redirect ends cleanly, instead of writing to a closed stream.
  • POST bodies set their size with the 64-bit libcurl option, which also works on Windows.
  • The scratch file of a download is created exclusively ("wbx").
  • The CSV splitter’s NUL branches are gone: under skipNul the NUL bytes are removed before the scan, so those branches could never run.
  • The README counts 123 C++ entry points, the comments in init.c name the right source files, and SECURITY.md names RtlGenRandom.
  • /dev/urandom is read through a descriptor opened close-on-exec instead of buffered stdio.
  • Native error messages are no longer cut at 1024 bytes by the barrier.
  • A wait for a lock held by another process ends at a Ctrl-C or a time limit.

Security

  • rmbl drift and rmbl refresh (cpschk(), cpsrfrsh()) fetch a capsule’s source over https:// only. A local path or a file:// URL is read only when it resolves, links followed, to a file inside the capsule, inside the allowfile folder (TRUE: the folder checked), or in the package’s extdata; never under /proc, /sys or /dev. A source such as /proc/self/environ or a creds.csv outside the capsule used to be printed in the report.
  • Drift reads the pinned data file only inside the capsule (resource$filename of ../../outside.csv was read and its header printed).
  • Refresh does not write through a data_provenance.json that links out of the capsule.
  • A gzip source or data file inflates to at most the option rmoriebricklayer.maxcsvbytes when drift or refresh reads it; a small gzip of zeros ran for minutes.
  • --public-key "" (or any capsule option given an empty value) is a usage error, and cpsbndlvrf() and cpschkatst() refuse keyexp = ""; both checked against no key.

Fixes from the audit of 30bed8e

  • fromjs() reads a \u escape only with four hex digits: \u 041 was read as “A” and \u-041 as the key “NA”.
  • A key typed in groups joined by any punctuation with no space (abcd1234efgh;ijkl5678mnop;...) is a key and is not sent to a model; so is an AWS access key id written in letters only.
  • RMBL_KEY is removed from the process before anything else, and its startup copy is wiped.
  • A provider reply with a long number or bytes that are not UTF-8 gives the package’s message, not R’s warnings.
  • wbsave() refuses a public name that resolves to a private address.
  • fromjs() decodes a latin1 string in a C locale, and simplifies sparse records about twice as fast.
  • fdl() passes a time limit on instead of trying the fallback; drift tries the Wayback copy the provenance pins and no other, and deletes its download.
  • The drift report escapes directory names in its HTML, and a symlink loop lists each capsule once.
  • Six test files of the native code (JSON parity, dtoa, HashML-DSA, sketches, the 1.0.0 native branches, X.509 branches) now also run on CRAN.

rmoriebricklayer 0.5.14

  • A new data key is issued only after the data access terms are accepted. rmbl login and bricklayer_llm_login() show the terms summary and their address, ask Do you accept ...? [y/N], and then ask for your name, organisation (optional) and why you need the data; for the restricted tables (Schedule B: ICPSR, NCVS 38604, A2AJ case law) they also ask for a supervisor, department chair, director or coordinator and their email. In a script, give them as arguments (accept_terms = TRUE, name, affiliation, purpose, restricted, supervisor_name, supervisor_role, supervisor_email) or flags (--accept-terms, --name, --affiliation, --reason, --restricted, --supervisor-name, --supervisor-role, --supervisor-email). Nothing is sent until every required answer is there; the data service checks the same things. login --token with a key you already hold is unchanged.

Fixes from the re-test of the b617a3f CRAN stress fixes

  • setTimeLimit() during a POST (ask, Wayback /save, the data-key check) is an ordinary error that tryCatch() catches, said as R says it (“reached elapsed time limit”); it halted Rscript as an interrupt. A Ctrl-C is still an interrupt.
  • A command typed as one argument is not a question: rmbl "cnfig set openai.key" and a tab-joined $'cnfig\tset\topenai.key' were sent to the first provider; they are a near miss now, named in “did you mean rmbl config”, with exit status 2 and nothing sent.
  • survey_design(): a JK1 replicate on a domain subset that scales every row by k / (k - 1) (its deleted PSU outside the subset; within 1% of the weight from 101 PSUs) is no longer refused as a copy; in a post-stratified or calibrated set, replicates equal or close to the weight are accepted and not warned about (bootstrap and BRR subsets were). A single JKn replicate equal to the weight is refused as the copy it is, and a JK1 or JKn replicate that leaves no row out without being such a rescale is warned about, as the Rd said.
  • A provider’s key prefix (sk-, gsk_, hf_, AIza, xai-, …) with twelve key characters or more is a key however short: a 23-character sk- key in a question went to a model.
  • survey_design(): a column of data passed in a partly named replicate matrix is refused as in a named one (it was taken as a replicate); two outcomes permuted for a permutation test beside columns still in place are no reorder (they were refused as one). Replicates given by name are no longer digested for the row check (the design keeps them): a design by name and each estimate on it were 2 to 5 times slower than the same replicates as a matrix (10.8 s and 7.8 s for 4.7 s and 1.5 s at a million rows). The adjustment check reads 4,096 rows of each replicate.
  • CSV reader parity with read.csv(): a byte-order mark at the start of the first row (after blank lines, or inside its opening quote) is dropped, as scan() drops it; a header of blanks or of the mark alone is a header of no columns, its rows read as row names.
  • Arguments: 123 functions gave a base R error for a value of the wrong kind (a data frame, a list, NA, a vector, a function or a number where a path goes), 696 cases in a battery of every export seeded from its examples; each is now an error that names the argument. Numeric arguments refuse lists, data frames, factors and complex numbers in words; the writers (yoy_csv() and the other yoy_*() writers, write_recode_manifest(), write_summary_txt(), use_capsule_template(), make_synthetic_csv(), bricklayer_download()) refuse a path that is not one string (a number was written as a file named 1); errors raised in the compiled code no longer carry the .Call().

rmoriebricklayer 0.5.13

  • The survey-estimation vignette loads the CSUS 2023 public-use file and its 1,000 mean bootstrap weights with bricklayer_data_load("csus_2023/pumf") and ("csus_2023/bootstrap"), now hosted on data.rmorie.com, or downloads them from Health Canada with bricklayer_download(); it no longer calls rmorie, which this package never depends on.
  • A new vignette, Causal effects with cross-fitted double machine learning: plr_crossfit() recovers a known effect on simulated data and, on the NSW job-training experiment (LaLonde 1986; Dehejia and Wahba 1999, hosted as nsw_dw/* on data.rmorie.com), moves the observational estimate against the PSID controls from -15,205 to 618 dollars, against the experimental 1,794.

Fixes from the CRAN stress test of b617a3f

  • A key next to punctuation never reaches a model. A question with no verb is refused as one when a key-shaped run appears anywhere in it (KEY?, "my key is KEY, thanks?", a key after a no-break or zero-width space), not only as a whole word: those went to the first provider, the wrong one for the key. Function names (bricklayer_json_base64url_dec) are not taken for keys. A verb typo with a ? apart (rmbl "doctr ?"), a leading ideographic space or quotes is a near miss, named in “did you mean”; a CJK question ending in a full-width question mark is asked.
  • survey_design(): genuine replicates passed by name are no longer refused when two of them are identical (216 of 2,400 test designs); JKn replicates of other strata, which equal the weight on a stratum subset, are accepted (every replicate equal to the weight is refused); a stratified bootstrap whose replicates equal the weight by chance, and post-stratified or calibrated jackknife subsets, are no longer warned about; a replicate a tenth of the weight’s scale (a normalised weight, a multiplier column) is said, as one ten times it was. Rows reordered and then a column dropped or one cell edited are refused (the SE was silently wrong); a row-name reset is accepted. The Rd says how to read the survey package’s own bootstrap replicates.
  • Interrupts and time limits: every POST polls for Ctrl-C and setTimeLimit(), not only when the wait label shows (Wayback /save, OCSP, the data-key check, ask with stderr redirected); a Ctrl-C in bricklayer_fetch() or wayback_snapshot_url_native() is raised at once instead of running the Wayback lookups on to their timeouts; the Wayback back-off without a terminal sleeps a second at a time, so a time limit ends it.
  • bricklayer_data_load() applies the option rmoriebricklayer.maxcsvbytes (1 GiB by default) on both of its read paths.
  • CSV reader parity with read.csv(): a line of NUL bytes is skipped; integers with leading zeros past ten characters are integers; a header of "" alone is a table of no columns; blanks outside a quoted header name are dropped; quotes after a closing quote are read as quotes; a header past a million fields is refused before it is held.
  • Language models: the last turn after the help-page lookups keeps the tools declared with calls turned off and rides on the last tool result (it was a second user turn with no tools, which Anthropic refuses); an SSE error event, or a 200 that carries an error, is said with its message; the saved-answer key includes a digest of the API key in use.
  • C and C++: argument errors and large allocations inside the entry points unwind through the barrier, so their buffers are freed (sen_slopes() leaked 858 MB at a failed allocation; small leaks in the HTTP header, gini, merkle, XMSS and BLAKE2b paths); a NaN or huge timeout is no longer cast to an integer (undefined behaviour).
  • Statistics: hurwitz_zeta(s, 1/2) is (2^s - 1) zeta(s), exact beside the trivial zeros; a point at -1e300 no longer collapses the Knox and hot-spot grids.
  • Arguments: a seed that is not one whole number is refused in words wherever a function seeds the RNG, and seeds now run from -2147483647 to 2^53 - 1: past set.seed()’s 32 bits the Mersenne-Twister state is built from the seed (each seed its own stream; seeds in the integer range give the stream they always did); lagrangian_particles(normals =) must be a function returning n finite numbers; a plot method given something its class’s function did not make says so.
  • SIU parsing of a long run of letters is linear (a 1 MB <p>AAAA... took four minutes; now 2.4 s).
  • The courts vignette’s case-mix paragraph is computed from its table; a test no longer writes Rplots.pdf into the tests directory; a complex-NA test follows R’s own coercion (it failed on R 4.3); the heaviest signature-vector blocks (about 100 s) are skipped on CRAN and run in CI.

Live progress for long work

  • bricklayer_progress(label, total), exported: the animated bar of bricklayer_download() for any loop, as an object with $update(done, info), $tick(by, info), $wait(seconds) and $done(summary). It follows the download bar’s rule (drawn while a person watches a terminal: an interactive session, or a command line that sets options(morie.progress = TRUE); a line at each tenth when stderr is not a terminal; nothing with options(morie.quiet = TRUE) or quiet = TRUE). Nothing is drawn for the first 0.75 s, so a fast call never flashes a bar; a bar inside another function’s running bar stays silent, so nested work shows the outer loop; an update is a stored value when quiet and a throttled frame when drawing. With total = 0 it is a spinner with the time so far and the current stage. on.exit(p$done(), add = TRUE) clears the line when the work fails or is interrupted.
  • Wired into the long-running functions: the bootstrap of exposure_response_plr(), the folds of plr_crossfit(), the permutations of knox_test() and step_change(), the controls of capsule_falsify(), the repetitions of capsule_power(), the splits of drift_calibrate(), the columns of capsule_drift(), profile_columns(), correlation_table() and top_correlations(), the stages of mahalanobis_outliers(), the EM iterations of mcar_test() and of core_hawkes_fit(method = "em"), the replicate checks of survey_design(), the steps of lagrangian_particles() and advection_diffusion_2d(), the receptors of gaussian_plume(), gaussian_puff() and plume_field(), the files of capsule_bundle() and capsule_bundle_verify(), the columns and the writing of make_synthetic_csv(), the packages of capture_dependencies(), the groups and exact p-values of analyse_table() and yoy_pvalues(), and long vectors in benford_test() and distinct_sketch() (read in blocks of a million; the counts and registers are those of one pass).
  • A spinner for long native calls: XMSS key generation and signing (pqc_keygen(), a few seconds at the default height, about a minute at 14), derive_key(), the native routes of core_hawkes_fit() (with the stage: first start, second start) and every network request (bricklayer_fetch(), the portal resolvers, wayback_snapshot_url_native(), revocation and service lookups, model lists) show a turning spinner with the label and the seconds so far, drawn by the compiled layer each time the call polls for a Ctrl-C, from 0.75 s on, on a terminal only. The XMSS tree now polls every 32 leaves (it was every 1,024, once in a whole default key).
  • Live progress in the IDE consoles, and one look for it. Whether a console can redraw a line is now decided as the cli package decides it, no longer by isatty(stderr()) alone, which is FALSE in the RStudio and Positron consoles, so most R users saw only the line at each tenth. Bars, spinners and the native spinner now animate in a terminal, the RStudio console (and its build and render panes), the Positron console, R.app and RKWard. They draw on stdout in the RStudio and Positron consoles, which print stderr in their error colour, and on stderr elsewhere. Colours follow the console (24-bit, 256, 8, or none; NO_COLOR, R_CLI_NUM_COLORS, RSTUDIO_CONSOLE_COLOR), and so does the width. They never animate inside knitr, an R Markdown notebook chunk or a Jupyter kernel, which get the plain lines. options(rmoriebricklayer.dynamic, rmoriebricklayer.numcol, rmoriebricklayer.unicode, rmoriebricklayer.width), cli’s options and R_CLI_DYNAMIC override the detection. The bar shows the percent, the count (or the bytes), the rate, the time so far and, once the rate has settled, the time left; it fits the console’s width and cuts the label or stage with an ellipsis. When the work ends, a green check, the label, the result and the time replace the bar; a red cross replaces it when the function that made the bar failed or was interrupted. bricklayer_download() shows the same cross. The native spinner of long compiled calls draws the same line, turns only on R’s main thread, ends with a check or a cross, and in a log writes a line at 0.75 s, one every ten seconds after it and one at the end.

Integrity scheme 2

New Merkle trees and chain entries are hashed under scheme 2 and record it; anything sealed by 0.5.12 or earlier (no scheme recorded) still verifies under its old rules, with a warning that it was sealed with the weaker scheme.

  • Merkle trees separate leaves from interior nodes (RFC 6962): a leaf is SHA-256 of the byte 0x00 and the chunk, a node SHA-256 of 0x01 and its two children. Under scheme 1 the 64 bytes of two sibling digests verified as a “leaf” with the shorter proof from their parent. merkle_root(), merkle_leaves() and merkle_proof() take scheme (2 by default; 1 recomputes a root pinned by an earlier version), merkle_proof() records it in the proof, and merkle_verify() reads it from there or takes scheme = 2 to refuse a proof without one. Roots therefore differ from those of 0.5.12 for the same chunks. capsule_report() records merkle_scheme beside merkle_root.
  • Chain entries cover their label. chain_append() records scheme = 2 and links "v2|<prev>|<payload>|<label>", so editing a label breaks the chain; under scheme 1 it went undetected.
  • Chain payloads no longer depend on the R version. A non-string entry is digested over serialize(version = 2) with the four header bytes naming the writer’s R version zeroed, so the same entry gives the same payload on every R version and for any R object.

Fixes

  • core_bootstrap_mean() draws its resamples with Lemire’s unbiased bounded draw on mt19937_64, as the reservoir sampler already does, instead of std::uniform_int_distribution, whose algorithm differs between libstdc++ and libc++: the same seed now gives the same resamples on Linux, Windows and macOS (the Linux and Windows results are unchanged). The means are summed in long double, so they still agree only to rounding between x86 and arm64.

  • Every conf_level goes through one check, with one message: trend_test(), count_trend(), analyse_table() and survey_compare() returned NaN intervals for a level outside (0, 1); case_flow(), life_table(), disposition_mix(), clearance_decomposition(), rate(), share(), rate_change(), yoy(), stay_summary() and survey_estimate() checked it in four different wordings. The interval helpers behind them refuse it too.

  • manifest_recompute() reports a statistic that returns NA, NaN or Inf as DIFFER (or MATCH when the record holds the identical value) instead of failing with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. record() refuses a vector observed or expected in words; it failed with R’s “‘length = 2’ in coercion to ‘logical(1)’”.

  • stock_flow() refuses a t that is neither one value nor one per period (it was recycled in silence) and a period of the wrong length; adp(), alos(), admissions(), adp_from_counts() and stock_flow()’s per refuse several values where one is meant (only the first was used).

  • profile_columns() leaves infinite values out of the mean, spread, range, quantiles and outlier count; they are still counted in n_infinite.

  • core_hawkes_fit() with the exponential kernel also runs from a second start and keeps the better optimum: from one start it could stop with the decay on its bound at a worse likelihood and still report converged = TRUE.

  • reservoir_indices() and reservoir_sample() draw with Lemire’s unbiased method on the raw 64-bit output of std::mt19937_64 instead of std::uniform_int_distribution, whose algorithm differs between C++ libraries: a seed now gives the same sample on Linux, macOS and Windows, and samples differ from those of 0.5.12. A seed that is NA, negative or fractional, and a fractional n or k, are refused (an NA seed was undefined behaviour in the cast).

  • core_bootstrap_mean() refuses an NA, negative or fractional seed and a fractional B (undefined behaviour in the casts), in R and in the compiled entry point; the compiled entry point of core_uniforms() now checks its seed too (its R function already did).

  • core_normal_logpdf() refuses a vector mean or sd and a non-positive sd, as core_normal_pdf() does; core_gamma_cdf(a, Inf) is 1, as pgamma(); core_trimmed_mean() and core_winsorized_mean() refuse a trim outside [0, 0.5] instead of returning NaN.

  • analyse_table() warns that rounding and suppression_limit apply only to counts when units is not "count"; they were ignored in silence.

  • Errors about a provenance list name load_provenance(); they named a read_provenance() that does not exist.

  • capture_dependencies() gives NA, not "", as the library of a package that is not installed, and the library of an installed one is the directory the package is in (it was its parent).

  • print() of a hot-spot persistence result names each period with its own count of tied cells (“period 2: 100 cells tied”); periods and counts were pasted into one list.

  • install_cli() refuses an empty or malformed name; an empty one printed “Installed ;” and failed with “subscript out of bounds”.

  • yoy_markdown() right-aligns every numeric column; the value and previous value were left aligned.

  • With direction = "neutral", print(), yoy_html(), yoy_pdf() and plot() of a change table draw rises and falls in the neutral colour; print(), yoy_html() and yoy_pdf() painted a rise in the bad colour, and plot() in the good one.

  • A malformed certificate, CRL, OCSP response or time-stamp token is an error without the call (cert_parse() errors read “Error in cert_parse(…)”).

  • Rd: [0, 1] in four help pages was read by roxygen as a link (an R CMD check warning for hotspot_persistence).

  • The “is thinking” line of a language-model call is drawn where the console says, on stdout in the RStudio and Positron consoles; it went to stderr, which they show in the error colour.

rmoriebricklayer 0.5.12

The 0.5.11 stress round (commit a5a4d10) and the review of this release’s own branch (head 6e80794, 2026-10-12): the findings of both fixed, each fix applied to its siblings, and the claims the earlier fixes overstated corrected.

Language models: bring your own key; the hosted tier is retired

  • Any major provider, or your own model. bricklayer_llm_ask() takes, in order, an endpoint of your own, then the first provider whose key is set, then Ollama. Sixteen providers are built in (bricklayer_llm_providers()): OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, Together AI, Fireworks AI, DeepSeek, Mistral, xAI, Cerebras, Perplexity, Hugging Face, OpenCode Zen, Cohere and NVIDIA, each from its usual key variable or a key saved privately with rmbl config set <provider>.key. Anthropic’s Messages API and Gemini’s generateContent are spoken natively, tool calls included; the others are OpenAI-compatible. route = "anthropic" (or any provider id) takes one route only; bricklayer_llm_models(route) and rmbl models --route list a route’s models; rmbl config setup asks for a provider, its key and its model.

  • The model knows the packages. With docs = TRUE (the default) the model is given the name, arguments and title of every function of the installed MORIE packages (rmoriebricklayer, and rmoriedata and rmorie when present), read from their installed help, and five read-only tools: a search over every help page, a help page, its examples, the dataset list and a vignette. A model that does not take tools gets the matching pages in its prompt. How much goes into the prompt follows the model’s context: everything for a provider’s model or an Ollama cloud model, the functions nearest the question for a model Ollama runs on this machine; MORIE_LLM_CONTEXT overrides. agent_bundle() asks the same way (its backend argument is now route).

  • bricklayer_llm_route_info() says which route would answer, without sending anything; bricklayer_llm_chat() sends a whole conversation as it is (no help, no tools), for chat loops in the other MORIE packages. rmorie’s help, thousands of pages, is searched by the tools, and only its functions nearest the question are listed for the model.

  • The hosted MORIE tier is retired. No route, setting or model list for it remains; route = "hosted" says so, and a saved hosted route falls back to the automatic order with a one-time message. Signing in (rmbl login) is for the curated tables at data.rmorie.com only, and rmbl doctor reports the data key.

  • A model the route does not have is named as such, with the number it has; a refused key is said as such, and the key never appears in an error.

  • The data key is checked and issued by the data service. login --token asks data.rmorie.com (/v1/whoami) whether it knows the key before storing it; the sign-in address is the services document’s data.auth_url, then its llm.auth_url for documents signed earlier.
